title: Inorganic Chemistry I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L inorganic chemistry curriculum, first semester: atomic structure, periodicity and periodic trends, chemical bonding, and the chemistry of hydrogen, s-block (Groups 1 and 2), and selected p-block elements (Groups 13-15). Transition metals, coordination chemistry, acid-base theories, and Groups 16-18 are reserved for CHM204 to keep the two courses distinct.

questions.question: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons fill atomic orbitals in which general order?
options: From lowest energy orbitals to higher energy orbitals
Always filling the 4s orbital after the 3d orbital
questions.correct_answer: From lowest energy orbitals to higher energy orbitals
questions.explanation: The Aufbau principle states that electrons occupy the lowest energy orbitals available before filling higher energy ones, building up the electron configuration of an atom.

questions.question: What does Hund's rule state about the filling of degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals, such as the three 2p orbitals?
options: Electrons singly occupy each degenerate orbital with parallel spins before any orbital is doubly occupied
Electrons must pair up in one orbital before occupying another of the same energy
Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing principal quantum number only
Degenerate orbitals cannot hold more than one electron in total
questions.correct_answer: Electrons singly occupy each degenerate orbital with parallel spins before any orbital is doubly occupied
questions.explanation: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing occurs, minimizing electron-electron repulsion.

questions.question: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in the same atom can have which characteristic?
options: The same set of all four quantum numbers
The same principal quantum number only
questions.correct_answer: The same set of all four quantum numbers
questions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle states that each electron in an atom must have a unique combination of the four quantum numbers (n, l, ml, ms), which is why an orbital holds a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

questions.question: What is the electron configuration of a chlorine atom (atomic number 17) in its ground state?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has 17 electrons, filling 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5, leaving one electron short of the stable noble gas (argon) configuration, consistent with its tendency to gain one electron.

questions.question: How does atomic radius generally change across a period from left to right in the periodic table?
options: It decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer without adding new shells
It increases steadily due to added electron shielding
It remains constant across the period
It increases because more protons repel each other
questions.correct_answer: It decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer without adding new shells
questions.explanation: Across a period, electrons are added to the same principal shell while nuclear charge increases, so the effective nuclear pull on the outer electrons increases, contracting the atomic radius.

questions.question: How does atomic radius generally change down a group in the periodic table?
options: It increases, because additional electron shells are added
It decreases due to increasing nuclear charge
It remains constant down the group
It fluctuates with no clear trend
questions.correct_answer: It increases, because additional electron shells are added
questions.explanation: Descending a group adds new electron shells further from the nucleus, and despite increased nuclear charge, the greater distance and shielding cause atomic radius to increase.

questions.question: What is ionization energy?
options: The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion
The energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom
The energy required to break a chemical bond
The energy released when a solid melts
questions.correct_answer: The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion
questions.explanation: First ionization energy is defined as the minimum energy required to remove the outermost (most loosely bound) electron from a neutral gaseous atom.

questions.question: Why is the second ionization energy of an atom always greater than its first ionization energy?
options: Removing an electron from an already positively charged ion requires more energy due to stronger electrostatic attraction
The second electron removed is always in a lower energy orbital
Ionization energy always decreases with each successive removal
There is no general difference between first and second ionization energies
questions.correct_answer: Removing an electron from an already positively charged ion requires more energy due to stronger electrostatic attraction
questions.explanation: Once one electron is removed, the resulting cation has a greater effective nuclear charge per remaining electron, making it harder to remove the next electron, so successive ionization energies increase.

questions.question: Electronegativity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Which element is considered the most electronegative on the periodic table?
questions.correct_answer: Fluorine
questions.explanation: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements (approximately 4.0 on the Pauling scale) due to its small atomic radius and high effective nuclear charge.

questions.question: What type of chemical bond is formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another?
questions.correct_answer: Ionic bond
questions.explanation: An ionic bond forms through the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions created by the transfer of electrons, typically between a metal and a non-metal.

questions.question: According to VSEPR theory, what is the molecular shape of methane (CH4), which has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around the central carbon atom?
questions.correct_answer: Tetrahedral
questions.explanation: VSEPR theory predicts that four bonding pairs with no lone pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.

questions.question: Why does a water molecule (H2O) have a bent (angular) shape rather than a linear shape, despite having only two bonding pairs?
options: The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle and bending the molecule
Water molecules are linear in the gas phase but bent in liquid form only
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules forces the bent shape
The bent shape is caused by the small size of hydrogen atoms only
questions.correct_answer: The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle and bending the molecule
questions.explanation: Oxygen in water has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs; because lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion, the molecule adopts a bent shape with a bond angle of about 104.5 degrees.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of a coordinate (dative) covalent bond, as seen in the formation of the ammonium ion NH4+?
options: Both shared electrons in the bond are donated by a single atom
The bond involves complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
The bond exists only between two identical atoms
The bond cannot be broken once formed
questions.correct_answer: Both shared electrons in the bond are donated by a single atom
questions.explanation: In a coordinate bond, one atom (the donor, such as the nitrogen lone pair in ammonia) supplies both electrons of the shared pair, unlike a normal covalent bond where each atom contributes one electron.

questions.question: Which theory describes metallic bonding as a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalized electrons?
options: Electron sea (delocalized electron) model of metallic bonding
Molecular orbital theory of covalent bonding
questions.correct_answer: Electron sea (delocalized electron) model of metallic bonding
questions.explanation: The electron sea model describes metals as a regular lattice of cations held together by freely moving delocalized valence electrons, explaining properties like electrical conductivity and malleability.

questions.question: Which of the following isotopes of hydrogen contains one proton and one neutron in its nucleus?
questions.correct_answer: Deuterium
questions.explanation: Deuterium (2H) has one proton and one neutron, protium (1H, ordinary hydrogen) has only a proton with no neutron, and tritium (3H) has one proton and two neutrons.

questions.question: Hydrogen can lose one electron to form H+ or gain one electron to form H-. This dual behaviour reflects hydrogen's unique position in the periodic table. What is the name given to the H- ion?
questions.correct_answer: Hydride ion
questions.explanation: When hydrogen gains an electron to achieve a helium-like electron configuration, it forms the hydride ion (H-), found in ionic hydrides such as NaH and CaH2.

questions.question: Which industrial method is commonly used to produce hydrogen gas on a large scale from natural gas (methane) and steam?
questions.correct_answer: Steam reforming of methane
questions.explanation: Steam reforming reacts methane with steam at high temperature over a catalyst to produce hydrogen gas and carbon monoxide, the major industrial source of hydrogen.

questions.question: Group 1 elements (alkali metals) are stored under oil. Why is this necessary?
options: They are highly reactive with oxygen and moisture in air
They are radioactive and must be shielded
They sublime rapidly at room temperature
They are extremely dense and sink in water
questions.correct_answer: They are highly reactive with oxygen and moisture in air
questions.explanation: Alkali metals react vigorously with both oxygen and water vapour in air, so they are stored under oil to exclude air and prevent unwanted reaction and oxidation.

questions.question: Why does reactivity of the alkali metals (Group 1) increase down the group, from lithium to caesium?
options: The outer electron is progressively further from the nucleus and more easily lost
The atomic radius decreases down the group, increasing reactivity
Nuclear charge decreases down the group
The number of valence electrons increases down the group
questions.correct_answer: The outer electron is progressively further from the nucleus and more easily lost
questions.explanation: Down Group 1, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding mean the single outer electron is held less tightly, so it is lost more easily, increasing reactivity.

questions.question: What is the general trend in thermal stability of Group 2 metal carbonates as you move down the group from magnesium to barium?
options: Thermal stability increases down the group
Thermal stability decreases down the group
Thermal stability remains exactly the same throughout
Group 2 carbonates are equally unstable regardless of position
questions.correct_answer: Thermal stability increases down the group
questions.explanation: As the cation size increases down Group 2, its polarizing power on the carbonate ion decreases, making the carbonate less easily decomposed by heat, so thermal stability increases down the group.

questions.question: Which Group 2 element's hydroxide is commonly used as 'milk of magnesia,' an antacid?
questions.correct_answer: Magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is a mild base used medicinally as an antacid and laxative, commonly known as milk of magnesia.

questions.question: Boron (Group 13) commonly forms compounds such as BF3 that are electron-deficient. What does 'electron-deficient' mean in this context?
options: The central atom has fewer than eight electrons in its valence shell
The molecule has no electrons at all around the central atom
The molecule is missing a proton in its nucleus
questions.correct_answer: The central atom has fewer than eight electrons in its valence shell
questions.explanation: Boron has only three valence electrons, so in compounds like BF3 it forms three bonds and has only six electrons around it, making it electron-deficient and a strong Lewis acid.

questions.question: Which allotrope of carbon consists of a three-dimensional network of tetrahedrally bonded carbon atoms, making it extremely hard?
questions.correct_answer: Diamond
questions.explanation: In diamond, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid tetrahedral three-dimensional lattice, giving diamond its extreme hardness, unlike the layered structure of graphite.

questions.question: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not, even though both are allotropes of carbon?
options: Graphite has delocalized electrons that move freely within its layered structure, while diamond's electrons are all localized in single bonds
Diamond contains free ions that block current flow
Graphite has more protons than diamond
Diamond is a liquid at room temperature while graphite is solid
questions.correct_answer: Graphite has delocalized electrons that move freely within its layered structure, while diamond's electrons are all localized in single bonds
questions.explanation: In graphite, each carbon is bonded to only three others within a layer, leaving one delocalized electron per atom free to move and conduct electricity along the layers; diamond's four localized sigma bonds leave no free electrons.

questions.question: Which allotrope of phosphorus is highly reactive, spontaneously flammable in air, and must be stored under water?
questions.correct_answer: White phosphorus
questions.explanation: White phosphorus is highly reactive and ignites spontaneously in air at room temperature, so it is stored under water to exclude oxygen; red phosphorus is far more stable and less reactive.

questions.question: In the industrial Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen combine to form ammonia. Which condition is used to increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia, consistent with Le Chatelier's principle?
options: High pressure, since the forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles
Low pressure, since it favours the side with fewer moles of gas
Constant volume with no pressure change required
Any pressure, since pressure has no effect on this equilibrium
questions.correct_answer: High pressure, since the forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles
questions.explanation: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 reduces the total moles of gas from 4 to 2, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the product side (ammonia), increasing yield.

questions.question: What is the shape of the ammonia (NH3) molecule according to VSEPR theory, given three bonding pairs and one lone pair on nitrogen?
questions.correct_answer: Trigonal pyramidal
questions.explanation: With three bonding pairs and one lone pair around nitrogen, the electron geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular shape (considering only atom positions) is trigonal pyramidal, with a bond angle slightly less than 109.5 degrees.

questions.question: Diagonal relationship in the periodic table describes similarity in properties between an element and the element diagonally below and to the right of it. Which pair shows a classic diagonal relationship?
questions.correct_answer: Lithium and magnesium
questions.explanation: Lithium (Group 1) and magnesium (Group 2) show a diagonal relationship, sharing similarities such as forming a nitride directly with nitrogen and having carbonates that decompose relatively easily on heating, due to similar charge density.

questions.question: What is the term for elements that have similar chemical and physical properties as a result of being in the same vertical column of the periodic table?
questions.correct_answer: A group (family)
questions.explanation: Elements in the same group (vertical column) have the same number of valence electrons and therefore tend to show similar chemical behaviour, such as the alkali metals in Group 1.

questions.question: Which type of intermolecular force is responsible for the unusually high boiling point of water compared to other Group 16 hydrides such as H2S?
questions.correct_answer: Hydrogen bonding
questions.explanation: Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds due to the high electronegativity of oxygen and the presence of O-H bonds, requiring significantly more energy to separate molecules, raising the boiling point well above that predicted from molecular mass alone.
